questions.stem: Psychology is best defined as the scientific study of:
options: the structure and chemistry of the brain
the history and customs of cultures
the mind and behaviour of individuals
society, its groups and its institutions
questions.explanation: Psychology studies the mind, behaviour and experiences of the individual. Sociology studies society, social groups and institutions.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four goals of psychology?
options: describe, understand, predict and control behaviour
observe, diagnose, treat and cure mental illnesses
measure, compare, rank and select individuals
question, debate, criticise and reform society
questions.explanation: Psychology aims to describe behaviour, understand (explain) why it happens, predict when it will happen, and control or influence it, for example through treatment.

questions.stem: A psychologist uses research on study habits to help students change how they revise, so they remember more. Which goal of psychology is this?
options: control (influence) behaviour
describe behaviour
predict behaviour
understand behaviour
questions.explanation: Applying knowledge to change behaviour is the goal of control or influence. Describing, understanding and predicting come first and make influencing behaviour possible.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that students who sleep less than seven hours tend to have lower test scores, and uses this to forecast which students may struggle. Which goal is she working towards?
options: description
control
diagnosis
prediction
questions.explanation: Using known relationships to forecast future behaviour is prediction. Describing would be recording sleep and scores; control would be changing them.

questions.stem: Empirical evidence is information that is:
options: drawn from personal opinion and common sense
passed down by tradition within a culture
gathered by objective observation or measurement
based on what most people believe to be true
questions.explanation: Empirical evidence is collected through systematic, objective observation and measurement, so others can check it. Psychology relies on it rather than on opinion or common sense.

questions.stem: Why do psychologists rely on empirical evidence rather than common sense?
options: Common sense is often contradictory or untested
Common sense is always wrong about human behaviour
Empirical evidence can never be questioned or revised
Empirical evidence comes only from case studies
questions.explanation: Common sense offers contradictory sayings (such as 'opposites attract' and 'birds of a feather flock together') and is rarely tested. Empirical evidence can be checked and revised as new data emerge.

questions.stem: Wilhelm Wundt is often called the founder of scientific psychology because, in 1879, he:
options: conducted the first study of conditioning in dogs
devised the first intelligence test for schools
set up the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig
published the first theory of psychoanalysis in Vienna
questions.explanation: Wundt's laboratory at the University of Leipzig is regarded as the start of psychology as a science separate from philosophy. Psychoanalysis was Freud's and conditioning in dogs was Pavlov's.

questions.stem: Wundt's main research method asked trained participants to report their own conscious experiences of stimuli. This method is called:
options: introspection
conditioning
psychoanalysis
observation
questions.explanation: Introspection means looking inward and reporting one's own sensations, thoughts and feelings. It was criticised because these reports cannot be checked by others, so they are subjective.

questions.stem: Before psychology became a science in the late 1800s, questions about the mind were mainly studied in:
options: neuroscience
economics
philosophy
sociology
questions.explanation: Philosophers from ancient Greece onwards, and later thinkers such as Descartes, debated the mind and its relationship to the body. Psychology emerged from philosophy and physiology.

questions.stem: John B. Watson argued in 1913 that psychology should study only behaviour that can be observed. This marked the start of:
options: humanism
structuralism
behaviourism
psychoanalysis
questions.explanation: Watson founded behaviourism, which rejected introspection and studied only observable behaviour and how it is learned from the environment.

questions.stem: Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic approach emphasised the role of:
options: the person's free will and personal growth
unconscious thoughts and childhood experiences
observable behaviour that is shaped by rewards
the computer-like processing of information
questions.explanation: Freud argued that unconscious desires and conflicts, often from early childhood, shape behaviour and personality. Free will and growth are humanist ideas.

questions.stem: Which sequence best orders these developments in the history of psychology, from earliest to latest?
options: Watson's behaviourism, Wundt's laboratory, the rise of cognitive psychology
the rise of cognitive psychology, Wundt's laboratory, Watson's behaviourism
Wundt's laboratory, the rise of cognitive psychology, Watson's behaviourism
Wundt's laboratory, Watson's behaviourism, the rise of cognitive psychology
questions.explanation: Wundt's laboratory opened in 1879, Watson launched behaviourism in 1913, and cognitive psychology grew from the 1950s and 1960s, partly in reaction to behaviourism's neglect of mental processes.

questions.stem: A researcher investigates how children's thinking changes between the ages of two and twelve. Which area of psychology is this?
options: memory and learning
mind, brain and body
psychological development
mental health
questions.explanation: Psychological development studies how people change physically, cognitively, socially and emotionally across the lifespan. A study of children's thinking over time belongs here.

questions.stem: A study of how anxiety disorders can be treated with therapy belongs to which area of psychology?
options: influences on behaviour
mental health
psychological development
memory and learning
questions.explanation: The area of mental health covers wellbeing, mental illness and its treatment. Anxiety disorders and therapy are central to this area.

questions.stem: A researcher examines how damage to the frontal lobe affects decision-making. Which area of study does this fit best?
options: influences on behaviour
mental health
mind, brain and body
psychological development
questions.explanation: The area of mind, brain and body studies how the brain and nervous system relate to thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Brain damage affecting decisions is a clear example.

questions.stem: In Australia, a person must be registered with which body to practise as a psychologist?
options: the Fair Work Commission
the Psychology Board of Australia
the Australian Medical Council
the Australian Bureau of Statistics
questions.explanation: Psychologists must be registered with the Psychology Board of Australia, through the national health practitioner agency (Ahpra), to use the title psychologist.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a psychiatrist and a psychologist in Australia?
options: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who can prescribe medication
A psychologist is a medical doctor who can prescribe medication
A psychiatrist studies only animals rather than human behaviour
A psychologist works only in research and never sees clients
questions.explanation: Psychiatrists complete a medical degree and then specialise in mental health, so they can prescribe medication. Psychologists study psychology and use assessment and talking therapies.

questions.stem: A psychologist works with athletes to manage pre-competition nerves and improve focus. This psychologist practises in:
options: sport and exercise psychology
forensic psychology
organisational psychology
clinical neuropsychology
questions.explanation: Sport and exercise psychologists help athletes with performance, motivation and anxiety. Forensic psychologists work with the legal system and organisational psychologists with workplaces.

questions.stem: A psychologist helps a company design a fairer staff selection process and reduce workplace stress. This is the work of:
options: a sport psychologist
an organisational psychologist
a clinical psychologist
a forensic psychologist
questions.explanation: Organisational psychologists apply psychology to workplaces, including selection, training, leadership and wellbeing. Clinical psychologists assess and treat mental illness.

questions.stem: A psychologist assesses whether an accused person is fit to stand trial and gives evidence in court. This psychologist works in:
options: health psychology
community psychology
forensic psychology
educational psychology
questions.explanation: Forensic psychologists apply psychology to the legal and criminal justice system, including assessments for courts and work with offenders and victims.

questions.stem: How does psychology's focus differ from sociology's?
options: Psychology uses only opinion; sociology uses only empirical evidence
Psychology studies only animals; sociology studies only humans
Psychology focuses on individuals; sociology on groups and society
Psychology focuses on society; sociology on the individual's mind
questions.explanation: Psychology explains the thoughts and behaviour of individuals, while sociology explains patterns in social groups, institutions and social change. Both are social sciences using empirical evidence.

questions.stem: A study asks why youth unemployment is higher in some regions than others and how it relates to the education system. Which discipline's approach does this mainly reflect?
options: sociology, because it examines patterns across social groups and institutions
psychology, because it examines one person's thoughts and feelings in depth
psychology, because unemployment is a mental illness studied by psychologists
sociology, because sociologists never use empirical evidence in their research
questions.explanation: Explaining patterns across regions and links with social institutions is sociological. A psychologist might instead study how unemployment affects an individual's wellbeing.

questions.stem: Psychology and sociology are described as 'distinct but not separate' disciplines. Which statement best explains this?
options: They study exactly the same things using exactly the same methods and theories
They have nothing in common, so their findings can never be compared
They are both branches of medicine that are practised in hospitals
They differ in focus but overlap in topics and both use scientific methods
questions.explanation: Psychology focuses on individuals and sociology on society, but they share topics such as socialisation, identity and behaviour in groups, and both seek empirical evidence.

questions.stem: The behaviourist perspective explains behaviour mainly in terms of:
options: mental processes such as memory and thinking
the influence of cultural values and social groups
learning from the environment through consequences
the structure and chemistry of the brain and body
questions.explanation: Behaviourists focus on observable behaviour and how it is learned through association and consequences such as rewards and punishments.

questions.stem: The cognitive perspective focuses on:
options: observable behaviour and the rewards that follow it
genes, hormones and the activity of the nervous system
the norms and values of a person's cultural group
mental processes such as memory and thinking
questions.explanation: The cognitive perspective studies how people take in, process, store and use information, often comparing the mind to an information-processing system.

questions.stem: A psychologist explains a person's depression in terms of low levels of certain neurotransmitters and a family history of the illness. Which perspective is being used?
options: cognitive
sociocultural
bio-psychological
behaviourist
questions.explanation: The bio-psychological perspective explains behaviour and mental processes in terms of the brain, nervous system, hormones and genetics. Neurotransmitters and family history are biological factors.

questions.stem: A psychologist explains why people in some cultures value group harmony over personal achievement. Which perspective is this?
options: behaviourist
cognitive
sociocultural
bio-psychological
questions.explanation: The sociocultural perspective examines how culture, social norms and the people around us shape thoughts and behaviour.

questions.stem: A student's fear of public speaking is explained as resulting from the thought 'everyone will think I'm stupid'. Which perspective does this explanation reflect?
options: behaviourist
bio-psychological
sociocultural
cognitive
questions.explanation: Focusing on the student's thoughts and beliefs is a cognitive explanation. A behaviourist explanation would focus on past experiences of punishment or reinforcement.

questions.stem: A child hits other children. Which explanation reflects the behaviourist perspective?
options: He believes other children are deliberately trying to annoy him
His community sees physical toughness as a sign of strength
Hitting has been rewarded because he gets the toys he wants
He has a gene that is linked to higher levels of aggression
questions.explanation: The behaviourist explanation focuses on learning through consequences: if hitting gets rewards, it becomes more likely. The others are bio-psychological, cognitive and sociocultural explanations.

questions.stem: A health psychologist studying why teenagers take up smoking draws on biological, cognitive, behaviourist and sociocultural explanations together. Why?
options: Only one perspective can ever be correct, so each must be tested in turn
Using several perspectives removes the need to collect empirical evidence
Each perspective applies only to children, so adults need all four of them
Behaviour usually has several causes, each captured in part
questions.explanation: Smoking involves nicotine dependence (biological), beliefs about stress relief (cognitive), learned habits (behaviourist) and peer and cultural influences (sociocultural). Combining perspectives gives a fuller explanation.

questions.stem: Which is usually the first step when a psychologist investigates a question scientifically?
options: drawing conclusions from the results
analysing the results statistically
defining the problem to be investigated
collecting data from the participants
questions.explanation: Scientific investigation begins by defining the problem, then reviewing the literature, proposing a hypothesis, choosing a design, collecting and analysing data, and drawing conclusions.

questions.stem: Psychology is considered a science mainly because it:
options: always studies behaviour in laboratory conditions
explains all behaviour in terms of brain chemistry
tests ideas systematically using empirical evidence
relies on the opinions of experienced practitioners
questions.explanation: A discipline is scientific when it tests ideas by gathering and analysing empirical evidence in a systematic, repeatable way. Not all psychological research is done in laboratories.

questions.stem: Using another person's words or ideas in an assignment without acknowledging them is called:
options: paraphrasing
citation
referencing
plagiarism
questions.explanation: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own. It breaches academic integrity, even when done accidentally.

questions.stem: A student summarises a journal article in her own words in her report. What must she still do?
options: nothing, because paraphrasing does not need a reference
put the whole summary in quotation marks as a direct quote
ask the author's permission before using the article at all
cite the article in the text and list it in her references
questions.explanation: Paraphrased ideas still belong to the original author, so they must be cited in the text and listed in the reference list. Quotation marks are used only for exact words.

questions.stem: Why is accurate referencing important in a psychology report?
options: It lets readers find and check the evidence for each claim
It makes the report longer so that it meets the word count
It shows that the student did not need to read any sources
It proves that every source used in the report is accurate
questions.explanation: References acknowledge the original authors and allow readers to locate and evaluate the evidence. They do not guarantee that the sources themselves are reliable.
